title: Perth 9pm weeknight trading (2010), re-evaluated with new data
design: Difference-in-differences with one treated state, on data the first evaluation did not use: retail business counts by place (metropolitan Perth against regional WA, retail against other industries, set against the same capital-versus-regional contrast in other states), monthly turnover of the general retail shops covered (WA against other states), and hours worked (descriptive).
comparison: Business counts: regional WA and capital-vs-rest gaps in NSW, Victoria, Queensland, Tasmania and the NT. Turnover: NSW, Victoria, Queensland and the ACT. SA excluded (Adelaide trading change in 2012).
window: Weeknight trading only: November 2010 to mid-2012, before Sunday trading began (26 Aug 2012). Business counts at 30 June 2009-2012; turnover monthly, July 2008 to July 2012.
grade_reason: One treated state caps the grade at Moderate. The plan's design checks pass for both primary outcomes and the business-count result holds in every robustness check; the turnover result does not (see caveats).
headline: Letting Perth's general retail shops open until 9pm on weeknights (November 2010) made no detectable difference to the number of retail businesses in Perth compared with regional WA (−1.8 log points, 90% interval −5.8 to +4.2) or to the turnover of supermarkets, clothing and department stores (+2.0%, −4.4 to +7.2). Effects of about 10% or more in either can be ruled out; smaller ones cannot.

category_summaries.competition: No detectable change in the number of retail businesses. Metropolitan Perth's retail business count moved −1.8 log points relative to regional WA and other industries (p = 0.70); small businesses alone −1.2.
category_summaries.productivity: No detectable change in sales, and the result is fragile. Turnover of the stores covered: +2.0% (p = 0.50). Hours worked are descriptive only: +1.6%.
category_summaries.prices: Not re-estimated. The first evaluation's food-price estimate reflected a trend that began before the reform.

outcomes.label: Retail businesses in metropolitan Perth relative to regional WA
outcomes.baseline_label: Retail businesses in metropolitan Perth, June 2010

outcomes.note: Perth minus rest-of-WA gap in log retail businesses, net of the same gap for other industries, against capital-vs-regional gaps in NSW, Victoria, Queensland, Tasmania and the NT. Small businesses only: −1.2; Mandurah in Perth: −2.1; WA outback left out: −1.6.

outcomes.label: Turnover of supermarkets, clothing and department stores
outcomes.baseline_label: WA turnover of these stores, $m a month, 2009-10

no_effect_range.basis: 90% range of 834 estimates at fake dates since 1995 and in comparison states

outcomes.note: WA against NSW, Victoria, Queensland and the ACT, monthly, seasonally adjusted. Two registered robustness checks reach p < 0.10 in opposite directions: removing each state's pre-reform trend gives +7.9 (p = 0.06); netting out cafes, restaurants and takeaway gives −19.3 (p = 0.09). The turnover result depends on the comparison.

caveats: Two registered robustness checks reach p < 0.10 in opposite directions: removing each state's pre-reform trend gives +7.9 (p = 0.06); netting out cafes, restaurants and takeaway gives −19.3 (p = 0.09). The turnover result depends on the comparison.
With one treated state, effects smaller than about 10% cannot be told apart from what happens without a reform.
Business counts are a proxy for competition: they show neither prices nor market shares, and only reach June 2012.
The turnover estimate does not net out WA-specific demand (the mining boom); the variant that does is the food-services comparison above.
Choices made at the design stage on hidden outcomes are listed in the plan (section 7), including outcomes dropped for lack of data (business exits inferred from names) or failed checks (hours).
